description: Climate chapter question bank derived point-by-point from Climate.pdf (FDA/SDA Competitive Examination Notes). Every distinct point converted once; no duplicates. Verify against latest official publications before formal use.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is weather?

options.A: The long-term statistical pattern of atmospheric conditions over 30 years
options.B: The day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time
options.C: The average rainfall of a region over a decade
options.D: The permanent climatic zone of a region

questions.explanation: Weather is the day-to-day condition of the atmosphere at a particular place and time, described through temperature, rainfall, humidity, wind, cloud cover and atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Climate is the long-term statistical pattern of weather conditions in a region, usually assessed over what period?

options.A: 10 years

questions.explanation: Climate is usually assessed over a 30-year period.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a climate normal?

options.A: A single year's weather record
options.B: A standard average of a climate variable calculated over a 30-year reference period

questions.explanation: A climate normal is a standard average of a climate variable calculated over a 30-year reference period.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following best states the difference between weather and climate?

options.A: Weather is long-term; climate is short-term
options.B: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term patterns, averages, variability and extremes
options.D: Weather refers only to rainfall; climate refers only to temperature

questions.explanation: Weather describes short-term atmospheric conditions; climate describes long-term patterns, averages, variability and extremes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major element of climate?

options.A: Temperature

questions.explanation: Major elements of climate are temperature, atmospheric pressure, wind, humidity, precipitation, cloud cover and sunshine.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a factor controlling the climate of a place?

options.A: Latitude

questions.explanation: Factors include latitude, altitude, distance from the sea, ocean currents, prevailing winds, relief/topography, vegetation and human land-use changes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the greenhouse effect?

options.A: The cooling of Earth's surface by atmospheric gases
options.B: The natural process in which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, keeping Earth's surface warmer
options.C: The reflection of sunlight by clouds
options.D: The depletion of the ozone layer by CFCs

questions.explanation: The greenhouse effect is the natural process in which greenhouse gases absorb and re-emit outgoing infrared radiation, keeping Earth's surface warmer than it would otherwise be.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is the natural greenhouse effect harmful?

options.A: Yes, it makes Earth uninhabitable
options.B: No, it makes Earth habitable; the enhanced greenhouse effect causes additional warming
options.C: Yes, it causes all climate change
options.D: No, it has no effect on temperature

questions.explanation: The natural greenhouse effect makes Earth habitable; the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by rising greenhouse-gas concentrations leads to additional warming.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate variability?

options.A: A permanent shift in climate
options.B: Natural or human-influenced fluctuations in climate conditions over seasons, years or decades
options.C: The average temperature of a region

questions.explanation: Climate variability refers to natural or human-influenced fluctuations in climate conditions over seasons, years or decades, such as variations in monsoon rainfall.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a climate extreme?

options.A: The average weather of a region
options.B: An unusually rare or severe value of a weather or climate variable compared with its local historical range

questions.explanation: A climate extreme is an unusually rare or severe value of a weather or climate variable compared with its local historical range, such as an extreme heatwave or intense rainfall.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between climate change and climate variability?

options.A: They are exact synonyms
options.B: Climate variability refers to fluctuations around the climate average; climate change refers to a persistent shift in the average state or variability over an extended period
options.C: Climate change is short-term; variability is long-term
options.D: Variability occurs only due to human activity

questions.explanation: Climate variability refers to fluctuations around the climate average; climate change refers to a persistent shift in the average state or variability of climate over an extended period.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate change?

options.A: A short-term weather fluctuation
options.B: A long-term change in the state of the climate, identifiable through changes in the mean and/or variability of its properties, persisting for decades or longer

questions.explanation: Climate change is a long-term change in the state of the climate, identifiable through changes in the mean and/or variability of its properties, persisting for decades or longer.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is anthropogenic climate change?

options.A: Climate change caused by volcanic eruptions
options.B: Climate change caused by human activities, especially greenhouse-gas emissions
options.D: Climate change caused by solar cycles

questions.explanation: Anthropogenic climate change is caused by human activities, especially greenhouse-gas emissions from fossil fuels, industry, agriculture, deforestation and land-use change.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which human activity is the largest source of carbon dioxide emissions globally?

options.A: Rice cultivation
options.B: Combustion of fossil fuels and industrial processes

questions.explanation: The combustion of fossil fuels and industrial processes, particularly energy production, transport and industry, is the largest source of CO₂ emissions globally.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is deforestation's contribution to climate change?

options.A: It increases carbon absorption by forests
options.B: It releases stored carbon, reduces the capacity of forests to absorb CO₂ and can alter local rainfall, temperature and water cycles
options.C: It has no effect on climate

questions.explanation: Deforestation releases stored carbon, reduces the capacity of forests to absorb carbon dioxide and can alter local rainfall, temperature and water cycles.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is the main evidence of climate change?

options.A: Rising global average temperatures, warming oceans, melting glaciers and sea-level rise

questions.explanation: Main evidence includes rising global average temperatures, warming oceans, melting glaciers and ice sheets, shrinking snow cover, sea-level rise, changing precipitation patterns and shifts in some extreme events and ecosystems.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is ocean acidification?

options.A: An increase in ocean pH
options.B: A decrease in ocean pH caused mainly by the absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Ocean acidification is a decrease in ocean pH caused mainly by the absorption of atmospheric carbon dioxide, which forms carbonic acid in seawater.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is ocean deoxygenation?

options.A: An increase in dissolved oxygen in oceans
options.B: A decline in dissolved oxygen in ocean waters, associated with warming, stratification and changes in circulation and biological processes
options.C: The formation of oxygen in the ocean

questions.explanation: Ocean deoxygenation is a decline in dissolved oxygen in ocean waters, associated with warming, stratification and changes in ocean circulation and biological processes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is sea-level rise mainly caused by?

options.A: Increased rainfall on land
options.B: Thermal expansion of warming seawater and addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets

questions.explanation: Sea-level rise is mainly due to thermal expansion of warming seawater and the addition of water from melting glaciers and ice sheets.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a climate tipping point?

options.A: A point where climate stops changing
options.B: A critical threshold beyond which a component of the Earth system may shift into a substantially different state with self-reinforcing, difficult-to-reverse consequences
options.D: A point where greenhouse gases are eliminated

questions.explanation: A climate tipping point is a critical threshold beyond which a component of the Earth system may shift into a substantially different state, potentially with self-reinforcing and difficult-to-reverse consequences.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate feedback?

options.A: A process that amplifies or reduces an initial climate change

questions.explanation: A climate feedback is a process that amplifies or reduces an initial climate change; positive feedback amplifies the change, while negative feedback counteracts it.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the ice-albedo feedback?

options.A: Melting ice exposes darker surfaces that absorb more solar energy, causing further warming and additional melting
options.B: Ice reflects more sunlight as it melts

questions.explanation: Melting ice exposes darker land or ocean surfaces that absorb more solar energy, causing further warming and additional melting.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is carbon sequestration?

options.A: The release of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere
options.B: The capture and long-term storage of carbon dioxide in forests, soils, geological formations or other reservoirs

questions.explanation: Carbon sequestration is the capture and long-term storage of carbon dioxide in forests, soils, geological formations or other reservoirs.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a carbon sink?

options.A: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a given period
options.B: A reservoir that releases more carbon than it absorbs

questions.explanation: A carbon sink is a natural or artificial reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases over a given period, such as a growing forest or some ocean systems.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a carbon source?

options.A: A reservoir that absorbs more carbon than it releases
options.B: A process or reservoir that releases more carbon into the atmosphere than it absorbs over a specified period

questions.explanation: A carbon source is a process or reservoir that releases more carbon into the atmosphere than it absorbs over a specified period.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between mitigation and adaptation?

options.A: Mitigation adjusts to impacts; adaptation reduces emissions
options.B: Mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases removals; adaptation adjusts human and natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts
options.D: Mitigation is only for developed countries

questions.explanation: Mitigation reduces greenhouse-gas emissions or increases removals; adaptation adjusts human and natural systems to actual or expected climate impacts.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are greenhouse gases (GHGs)?

options.A: Atmospheric gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, contributing to the greenhouse effect
options.B: Gases that deplete the ozone layer only
options.C: Gases that cause acid rain only

questions.explanation: Greenhouse gases are atmospheric gases that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, contributing to the greenhouse effect.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major greenhouse gas listed in the notes?

options.A: Carbon dioxide

questions.explanation: Major GHGs are CO₂, CH₄, N₂O, water vapour, ozone and fluorinated gases such as HFCs, PFCs, SF₆ and NF₃.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which greenhouse gas is most associated with fossil-fuel combustion?

options.A: Methane

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is most associated with fossil-fuel combustion.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is a major source of methane?

options.A: Livestock digestion and manure, rice cultivation, landfills, wastewater, coal mining and oil-and-gas extraction

questions.explanation: Major methane sources include livestock digestion and manure, rice cultivation, landfills, wastewater, coal mining and oil-and-gas extraction and distribution.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are the major sources of nitrous oxide?

options.A: Agricultural soils and nitrogen fertilisers, manure management, some industrial processes and fuel combustion

questions.explanation: Major sources of nitrous oxide are agricultural soils and nitrogen fertilisers, manure management, some industrial processes and fuel combustion.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which greenhouse gas is emitted in large quantities from cement manufacture?

options.A: Methane

questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide is released both from fuel use and from the chemical calcination of limestone in cement manufacture.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is global warming potential (GWP)?

options.A: A measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a specified time horizon relative to the same mass of carbon dioxide
options.B: The total amount of a gas in the atmosphere
options.C: The lifetime of a gas in the atmosphere

questions.explanation: GWP is a measure of how much heat a greenhouse gas traps over a specified time horizon relative to the same mass of carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e)?

options.A: A unit that expresses the warming impact of different greenhouse gases as an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide
options.B: The mass of carbon in a fuel
options.C: The amount of CO₂ dissolved in oceans

questions.explanation: CO₂e is a common unit that expresses the warming impact of different greenhouse gases as an equivalent amount of carbon dioxide.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Is water vapour the main driver of current human-caused global warming?

options.A: Yes, it is the primary driver
options.B: No, water vapour is an important greenhouse gas and climate feedback, but the long-term rise is driven primarily by human emissions of long-lived greenhouse gases, especially CO₂
options.C: Yes, because it is the most abundant gas
options.D: No, water vapour has no greenhouse effect

questions.explanation: Water vapour is an important greenhouse gas and climate feedback, but the long-term rise in global temperature is driven primarily by human emissions of long-lived greenhouse gases, especially CO₂.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect agriculture?

options.A: It improves all crop yields uniformly
options.B: It can alter growing seasons, crop yields, pest and disease patterns, soil moisture, irrigation demand and monsoon reliability
options.C: It has no effect on agriculture

questions.explanation: Climate change can alter growing seasons, crop yields, pest and disease patterns, soil moisture, irrigation demand and the reliability of monsoon rainfall.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect water resources?

options.A: It changes rainfall and runoff patterns, increases evaporation, affects groundwater recharge and snow/glacier melt, and can intensify both drought and flood risks
options.C: It has no effect on groundwater

questions.explanation: Climate change changes rainfall and runoff patterns, increases evaporation, affects groundwater recharge and snow/glacier melt, and can intensify both drought and flood risks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect human health?

options.A: It reduces all health risks
options.B: It increases heat stress and can worsen risks from vector-borne and water-borne diseases, malnutrition, respiratory illness and disaster-related injuries

questions.explanation: Climate change increases heat stress and can worsen risks from vector-borne and water-borne diseases, malnutrition, respiratory illness and disaster-related injuries.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect biodiversity?

options.A: It shifts habitats and species ranges, alters breeding and migration cycles, increases stress on ecosystems and can raise extinction risks
options.C: It has no effect on species

questions.explanation: Climate change shifts habitats and species ranges, alters breeding and migration cycles, increases stress on ecosystems and can raise extinction risks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect coastal areas?

options.A: Sea-level rise, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion, storm surges and changing marine ecosystems can threaten settlements, agriculture, infrastructure and livelihoods
options.C: It has no effect on coastal areas

questions.explanation: Sea-level rise, coastal erosion, saltwater intrusion, storm surges and changing marine ecosystems can threaten settlements, agriculture, infrastructure and livelihoods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does climate change affect the Himalayan region?

options.A: It contributes to glacier and snow changes, altered water availability, slope instability and risks from glacial lake outburst floods
options.B: It has no effect on Himalayan glaciers

questions.explanation: Climate change contributes to glacier and snow changes, altered water availability, slope instability and risks from glacial lake outburst floods, alongside other regional drivers.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Can climate change cause both droughts and floods?

options.A: No, it causes only droughts
options.C: Yes; a warmer atmosphere can intensify the hydrological cycle, producing longer dry spells in some periods or places and heavier downpours in others
options.D: No, droughts and floods are unrelated to climate

questions.explanation: A warmer atmosphere can intensify the hydrological cycle, while changing circulation and rainfall patterns can produce longer dry spells in some periods or places and heavier downpours in others.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is global warming?

options.A: The long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily due to the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activities

questions.explanation: Global warming is the long-term rise in Earth's average surface temperature, primarily due to the enhanced greenhouse effect caused by human activities.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How is global warming different from climate change?

options.A: They are exact synonyms
options.B: Global warming refers specifically to the increase in average temperature; climate change is broader and includes changes in rainfall, winds, oceans, ice, sea level and extremes
options.C: Global warming is broader than climate change
options.D: Climate change refers only to temperature

questions.explanation: Global warming refers specifically to the increase in average temperature; climate change is broader and includes changes in rainfall, winds, oceans, ice, sea level and extremes.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which pre-industrial reference period is commonly used in climate discussions?
questions.explanation: The period 1850–1900 is commonly used as an approximation of pre-industrial global temperature.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Paris Agreement temperature goal?

options.A: To hold the increase to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C

questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement aims to hold the increase in global average temperature to well below 2°C above pre-industrial levels and pursue efforts to limit it to 1.5°C.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why is the 1.5°C limit important?

options.A: Every additional increment of warming increases risks; limiting warming to 1.5°C rather than 2°C reduces many climate-related risks and impacts, though it does not eliminate them
options.D: It applies only to developed countries

questions.explanation: Every additional increment of warming increases risks; limiting warming to 1.5°C rather than 2°C reduces many climate-related risks and impacts, though it does not eliminate them.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a heatwave?

options.A: A period of abnormally high temperatures relative to local climatological conditions, lasting several days
options.C: A period of unusually low temperatures

questions.explanation: A heatwave is a period of abnormally high temperatures relative to the local climatological conditions, lasting for several days; operational criteria are defined by the national meteorological agency.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does a cold wave disprove global warming?

options.A: Yes, cold waves prove Earth is cooling
options.B: No, global warming concerns long-term global averages; cold events can still occur in particular regions and seasons
options.C: Yes, cold waves are incompatible with warming
options.D: No, because cold waves do not exist

questions.explanation: Global warming concerns long-term global averages; cold events can still occur in particular regions and seasons.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the urban heat island effect?

options.A: The tendency of built-up urban areas to be warmer than nearby rural areas because of heat-absorbing surfaces, reduced vegetation, waste heat and urban form
options.B: The cooling of cities relative to rural areas
options.D: A phenomenon occurring only in coastal cities

questions.explanation: The urban heat island effect is the tendency of built-up urban areas to be warmer than nearby rural areas because of heat-absorbing surfaces, reduced vegetation, waste heat and urban form.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is black carbon?

options.A: A light-absorbing component of particulate matter produced by incomplete combustion that contributes to atmospheric warming and can accelerate snow and ice melt

questions.explanation: Black carbon is a light-absorbing component of particulate matter produced by incomplete combustion; it contributes to atmospheric warming and can accelerate snow and ice melt when deposited on them.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the role of oceans in global warming?

options.A: Oceans absorb most of the excess heat accumulated in the climate system and a substantial share of human-emitted carbon dioxide
options.B: Oceans release all their heat to the atmosphere
options.C: Oceans do not interact with the climate system

questions.explanation: Oceans absorb most of the excess heat accumulated in the climate system and a substantial share of human-emitted carbon dioxide, influencing climate and sea level.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the UNFCCC?

options.A: The United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change, adopted in 1992 and in force since 1994

questions.explanation: The UNFCCC was adopted in 1992 at the Rio Earth Summit and entered into force in 1994; it provides the main international framework for climate negotiations.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the ultimate objective of the UNFCCC?

options.A: To stabilise greenhouse-gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that prevents dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system
options.B: To eliminate all greenhouse gases immediately

questions.explanation: The ultimate objective of the UNFCCC is to stabilise greenhouse-gas concentrations in the atmosphere at a level that prevents dangerous anthropogenic interference with the climate system.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Kyoto Protocol?

options.A: A 1997 protocol to the UNFCCC that established legally binding emission-reduction targets for developed-country Parties

questions.explanation: The Kyoto Protocol is a 1997 protocol to the UNFCCC that established legally binding emission-reduction targets for developed-country Parties during its commitment periods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in which year?
questions.explanation: The Paris Agreement was adopted at COP21 in Paris in 2015 and entered into force in 2016.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What are Nationally Determined Contributions (NDCs)?

options.A: National climate action plans submitted by Parties under the Paris Agreement, setting out mitigation and, where appropriate, adaptation commitments
options.B: Binding emission targets for developed countries only

questions.explanation: NDCs are national climate action plans submitted by Parties under the Paris Agreement, setting out their mitigation and, where appropriate, adaptation commitments.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is COP in climate negotiations?

options.A: The Conference of the Parties, the supreme decision-making body of the UNFCCC

questions.explanation: COP is the Conference of the Parties, the supreme decision-making body of the UNFCCC.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Where was COP28 held in 2023?

options.A: Baku, Azerbaijan

questions.explanation: COP28 was held in Dubai, United Arab Emirates, in 2023.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Where was COP29 held in 2024?

options.A: Dubai, UAE

questions.explanation: COP29 was held in Baku, Azerbaijan, in 2024.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Where was COP30 held in 2025?

options.A: Dubai, UAE

questions.explanation: COP30 was held in Belem, Brazil, in 2025.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the principle of Common but Differentiated Responsibilities and Respective Capabilities (CBDR-RC)?

options.A: All countries share responsibility, but responsibilities and efforts should reflect differences in historical contributions, national circumstances and capabilities

questions.explanation: All countries share responsibility for addressing climate change, but responsibilities and efforts should reflect differences in historical contributions, national circumstances and capabilities.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate finance?

options.A: Financial resources provided or mobilised to support mitigation and adaptation actions, particularly in developing countries

questions.explanation: Climate finance refers to financial resources provided or mobilised to support mitigation and adaptation actions, particularly in developing countries.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is loss and damage in climate policy?

options.A: Climate-related harms that occur when mitigation and adaptation are insufficient or limits are reached, including economic and non-economic losses

questions.explanation: Loss and damage refers to climate-related harms that occur when mitigation and adaptation are insufficient or limits are reached; they may include economic and non-economic losses.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Green Climate Fund (GCF)?

options.A: An international climate fund established under the UNFCCC to support developing countries in low-emission and climate-resilient development
options.B: A World Bank fossil fuel fund

questions.explanation: The GCF is an international climate fund established under the UNFCCC to support developing countries in low-emission and climate-resilient development.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC)?

options.A: The UN body established in 1988 by WMO and UNEP to assess scientific knowledge on climate change

questions.explanation: The IPCC is the UN body established in 1988 by the World Meteorological Organization and the United Nations Environment Programme to assess scientific knowledge on climate change.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does the IPCC conduct its own climate experiments?

options.A: Yes, it runs global climate models
options.B: No, it assesses and synthesises published scientific literature and does not normally conduct original research or monitor climate directly
options.C: Yes, it monitors weather stations worldwide

questions.explanation: The IPCC assesses and synthesises published scientific literature; it does not normally conduct original research or monitor climate directly.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an extreme weather event?

options.A: A weather event that is rare or unusually severe for a particular place and time of year

questions.explanation: An extreme weather event is a weather event that is rare or unusually severe for a particular place and time of year, such as a heatwave, intense rainfall, cyclone, drought or severe storm.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT listed as a major type of extreme weather event?

options.A: Heatwaves

questions.explanation: Listed types include heatwaves, cold waves, heavy rainfall, floods, droughts, tropical cyclones, thunderstorms, lightning, hailstorms, cloudbursts, storm surges and rainfall-triggered landslides. Earthquakes are not weather events.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a cloudburst?

options.A: An episode of exceptionally intense rainfall over a small area in a short period; the IMD operational threshold is about 100 mm or more in one hour

questions.explanation: A cloudburst is an episode of exceptionally intense rainfall over a small area in a short period; the commonly used IMD operational threshold is about 100 mm or more in one hour.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a tropical cyclone?

options.A: A rotating low-pressure weather system developing over warm tropical or subtropical waters, with organised thunderstorms and strong winds
options.B: A high-pressure system over cold waters

questions.explanation: A tropical cyclone is a rotating low-pressure weather system developing over warm tropical or subtropical waters, with organised thunderstorms and strong winds.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a storm surge?

options.A: An abnormal rise of sea level near a coast caused mainly by a cyclone's strong winds and low atmospheric pressure
options.B: A sudden drop in sea level

questions.explanation: A storm surge is an abnormal rise of sea level near a coast caused mainly by a cyclone's strong winds and low atmospheric pressure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is lightning?

options.A: A sudden electrostatic discharge occurring within clouds, between clouds or between a cloud and the ground

questions.explanation: Lightning is a sudden electrostatic discharge occurring within clouds, between clouds or between a cloud and the ground.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a thunderstorm?

options.A: A storm associated with cumulonimbus clouds, usually accompanied by lightning and thunder, and possibly heavy rain, gusty winds or hail

questions.explanation: A thunderstorm is a storm associated with cumulonimbus clouds and usually accompanied by lightning and thunder; it may also produce heavy rain, gusty winds or hail.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a landslide?

options.A: The downward movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity; intense rainfall, slope cutting, earthquakes and land-use change can trigger or worsen it

questions.explanation: A landslide is the downward movement of rock, soil or debris under gravity; intense rainfall, slope cutting, earthquakes and land-use change can trigger or worsen it.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an El Niño event?

options.A: A periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that can influence global weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon
options.B: A periodic cooling of the Pacific Ocean
options.C: A warming of the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: El Niño is a periodic warming of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean that can influence global weather patterns, including the Indian monsoon.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is La Niña?

options.A: A periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, often associated with different global circulation patterns from El Niño
options.B: A warming of the Pacific Ocean
options.C: A warming of the Indian Ocean

questions.explanation: La Niña is a periodic cooling of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific Ocean, often associated with different global circulation patterns from El Niño.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Does El Niño always cause drought in India?

options.A: Yes, always
options.B: No; it raises the probability of a weaker Indian summer monsoon in many years, but the actual outcome also depends on other ocean-atmosphere factors and regional conditions

questions.explanation: El Niño raises the probability of a weaker Indian summer monsoon in many years, but the actual outcome also depends on other ocean-atmosphere factors and regional conditions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Indian Ocean Dipole (IOD)?

options.A: A climate pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperatures between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean, whose phases can influence monsoon rainfall

questions.explanation: The IOD is a climate pattern involving differences in sea-surface temperatures between the western and eastern tropical Indian Ocean; its positive and negative phases can influence monsoon rainfall.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Madden-Julian Oscillation (MJO)?

options.A: A large-scale eastward-moving pattern of tropical rainfall and atmospheric circulation that can influence monsoon activity and tropical cyclone formation

questions.explanation: The MJO is a large-scale eastward-moving pattern of tropical rainfall and atmospheric circulation that can influence monsoon activity and tropical cyclone formation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Which agency is India's principal national weather forecasting authority?

options.A: The India Meteorological Department (IMD), under the Ministry of Earth Sciences

questions.explanation: The India Meteorological Department (IMD), under the Ministry of Earth Sciences, is India's principal national weather forecasting authority.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Which agency coordinates disaster management at the national level in India?

options.A: The National Disaster Management Authority (NDMA), established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005

questions.explanation: The NDMA, established under the Disaster Management Act, 2005, coordinates disaster management at the national level.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: What is the role of the IMD in extreme-weather management?

options.A: It monitors weather, issues forecasts and warnings for cyclones, heavy rainfall, heatwaves and thunderstorms, and provides meteorological information to authorities and the public

questions.explanation: The IMD monitors weather, issues forecasts and warnings for events such as cyclones, heavy rainfall, heatwaves and thunderstorms, and provides meteorological information to authorities and the public.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: In the IMD's colour-coded warning system, what does 'red' indicate?

options.A: No warning

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Which parts of Karnataka are vulnerable to intense monsoon rainfall and floods?

options.A: The coastal belt, Western Ghats and adjoining Malnad districts

questions.explanation: The coastal belt, Western Ghats and adjoining Malnad districts are particularly exposed to heavy monsoon rainfall, flash floods and landslides.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Which parts of Karnataka are relatively drought-prone?

options.A: The coastal belt and Western Ghats
options.B: The rain-shadow and semi-arid interior districts, particularly parts of northern and eastern Karnataka

questions.explanation: The rain-shadow and semi-arid interior districts, particularly parts of northern and eastern Karnataka, are vulnerable to recurrent rainfall deficits and agricultural drought.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Why is Bengaluru vulnerable to urban flooding?

options.A: Rapid urbanisation, encroachment or loss of lake and wetland systems, reduced infiltration, obstruction of natural drainage, impervious surfaces and intense short-duration rainfall can combine to cause urban floods
options.B: Because it receives the highest rainfall in India
options.C: Because it is located on the coast
options.D: Because it has no drainage systems at all

questions.explanation: Rapid urbanisation, encroachment or loss of lake and wetland systems, reduced infiltration, obstruction of natural drainage, impervious surfaces and intense short-duration rainfall can combine to cause urban floods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: What is the urban heat island concern in Bengaluru?

options.A: Dense construction, traffic, waste heat, reduced tree cover and extensive paved surfaces can increase local heat exposure
options.B: Bengaluru is cooler than surrounding rural areas
options.D: The urban heat island effect occurs only in coastal cities

questions.explanation: Dense construction, traffic, waste heat, reduced tree cover and extensive paved surfaces can increase local heat exposure in Bengaluru.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Which Karnataka region is especially vulnerable to coastal climate risks?

options.A: The Arabian Sea coastal districts of Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada

questions.explanation: The Arabian Sea coastal districts of Dakshina Kannada, Udupi and Uttara Kannada face risks including coastal erosion, sea-level rise, storm impacts and saline intrusion.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.chapter: Extreme Weather in India and Karnataka
questions.question: Why are the Western Ghats environmentally important in climate regulation?

options.A: They influence orographic rainfall, support high biodiversity, regulate catchments and provide ecosystem services important for water security and climate resilience
options.B: They are the largest desert in India
options.C: They have no role in rainfall
options.D: They are located in the Bay of Bengal

questions.explanation: The Western Ghats influence orographic rainfall, support high biodiversity, regulate catchments and provide ecosystem services important for water security and climate resilience.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is drought?

options.A: A prolonged period of abnormally low water availability caused by a rainfall deficit and/or increased water demand
options.C: A long-term climatic characteristic of a dry region

questions.explanation: Drought is a prolonged period of abnormally low water availability caused by a rainfall deficit and/or increased water demand, affecting water resources, agriculture, ecosystems and society.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is meteorological drought?

options.A: A situation in which precipitation is significantly below the long-term normal for a specified period and area
options.B: Insufficient soil moisture during the growing season
options.C: A prolonged deficiency in surface water and groundwater
options.D: A water shortage affecting economic activity

questions.explanation: Meteorological drought is a situation in which precipitation is significantly below the long-term normal for a specified period and area.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is agricultural drought?

options.A: A situation in which soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop water requirements during the growing season
options.B: A rainfall deficit over a large area
options.C: A deficiency in river flows and reservoir storage

questions.explanation: Agricultural drought is a situation in which soil moisture is insufficient to meet crop water requirements during the growing season.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is hydrological drought?

options.A: A prolonged deficiency in surface water and groundwater levels, including low river flows, reservoir storage and aquifer levels
options.B: A rainfall deficit over a small area

questions.explanation: Hydrological drought is a prolonged deficiency in surface water and groundwater levels, including low river flows, reservoir storage and aquifer levels.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is socio-economic drought?

options.A: A situation in which water shortage affects the supply of goods and services, livelihoods and economic activity

questions.explanation: Socio-economic drought is a situation in which water shortage affects the supply of goods and services, livelihoods and economic activity.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is ecological drought?

options.A: A prolonged and widespread deficit in naturally available water that creates ecosystem stress and threatens ecological functions
options.B: A rainfall deficit over a city
options.C: A soil moisture deficit in farmland

questions.explanation: Ecological drought is a prolonged and widespread deficit in naturally available water that creates ecosystem stress and threatens ecological functions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is flash drought?

options.A: A rapid-onset drought that develops over a short period, often due to unusually high temperatures, low rainfall and rapid soil-moisture loss
options.B: A drought that lasts for decades
options.C: A drought caused only by groundwater depletion
options.D: A drought affecting only coastal areas

questions.explanation: Flash drought is a rapid-onset drought that develops over a short period, often due to unusually high temperatures, low rainfall and rapid soil-moisture loss.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major cause of drought listed in the notes?

options.A: Deficient or delayed rainfall

questions.explanation: Major causes include deficient or delayed rainfall, prolonged dry spells, high temperatures and evaporation, El Niño-related circulation patterns, land degradation, deforestation, unsustainable groundwater extraction and poor water management.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between drought and aridity?

options.A: Drought is a temporary or episodic water deficit; aridity is a long-term climatic characteristic of a dry region
options.B: Drought is long-term; aridity is temporary
options.D: Aridity occurs only in coastal areas

questions.explanation: Drought is a temporary or episodic water deficit; aridity is a long-term climatic characteristic of a dry region.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between drought and famine?

options.A: Drought is a climatic or hydrological hazard; famine is an extreme human food-security crisis that may arise from drought and other factors, including conflict, poverty and market failure
options.B: Drought and famine are the same
options.C: Famine is a climatic hazard; drought is a food crisis

questions.explanation: Drought is a climatic or hydrological hazard; famine is an extreme human food-security crisis that may arise from drought and other factors, including conflict, poverty and market failure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Standardised Precipitation Index (SPI)?

options.A: An index that expresses observed precipitation deficits or surpluses relative to the historical probability distribution for a chosen time scale
options.B: An index that considers precipitation and atmospheric evaporative demand
options.C: A measure of soil moisture only

questions.explanation: SPI expresses observed precipitation deficits or surpluses relative to the historical probability distribution for a chosen time scale.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the Standardised Precipitation Evapotranspiration Index (SPEI)?

options.A: A drought index that considers the balance between precipitation and atmospheric evaporative demand
options.B: An index based only on precipitation

questions.explanation: SPEI is a drought index that considers the balance between precipitation and atmospheric evaporative demand.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is evapotranspiration?

options.A: The combined transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration by plants
options.B: The movement of water into the soil
options.C: The flow of water in rivers

questions.explanation: Evapotranspiration is the combined transfer of water to the atmosphere through evaporation from surfaces and transpiration by plants.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a rain-shadow region?

options.A: An area on the leeward side of a mountain range that receives less rainfall because much of the moist air has already lost its moisture on the windward side
options.B: An area on the windward side of a mountain range
options.C: A coastal area with heavy rainfall

questions.explanation: A rain-shadow region is an area on the leeward side of a mountain range that receives less rainfall because much of the moist air has already lost its moisture on the windward side.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is a major effect of drought?

options.A: Crop failure, livestock distress, drinking-water shortages, groundwater depletion, food-price increases, rural unemployment, migration, malnutrition, ecosystem damage and conflict over scarce resources

questions.explanation: Major effects include crop failure, livestock distress, drinking-water shortages, groundwater depletion, food-price increases, rural unemployment, migration, malnutrition, ecosystem damage and conflict over scarce resources.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does drought affect farmers?

options.A: It reduces soil moisture and crop yields, raises irrigation costs, increases crop failure risk and can lead to debt and loss of income

questions.explanation: Drought reduces soil moisture and crop yields, raises irrigation costs, increases crop failure risk and can lead to debt and loss of income.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is drought preparedness?

options.A: Advance planning through monitoring, contingency crop plans, water budgeting, fodder banks, drinking-water arrangements, early warning and institutional coordination
options.B: Responding only after a drought has occurred

questions.explanation: Drought preparedness involves advance planning through monitoring, contingency crop plans, water budgeting, fodder banks, drinking-water arrangements, early warning and institutional coordination.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is watershed management?

options.A: Integrated management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage area to conserve soil and water, reduce runoff and improve local water availability

questions.explanation: Watershed management is the integrated management of land, water and vegetation within a drainage area to conserve soil and water, reduce runoff and improve local water availability.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How do check dams help in drought-prone areas?

options.A: They slow surface runoff, reduce erosion and can improve local groundwater recharge where site conditions are suitable

questions.explanation: Check dams slow surface runoff, reduce erosion and can improve local groundwater recharge where site conditions are suitable.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How does micro-irrigation help reduce drought vulnerability?

options.A: Drip and sprinkler systems can improve water-use efficiency and deliver water more precisely than many conventional surface-irrigation methods
options.D: It requires more water than flood irrigation

questions.explanation: Drip and sprinkler systems can improve water-use efficiency and deliver water more precisely than many conventional surface-irrigation methods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is drought-resistant agriculture?

options.A: Agricultural practices that reduce crop sensitivity to water stress through suitable varieties, crop diversification, soil-moisture conservation, altered sowing dates and efficient irrigation

questions.explanation: Drought-resistant agriculture reduces crop sensitivity to water stress through suitable varieties, crop diversification, soil-moisture conservation, altered sowing dates and efficient irrigation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is contingency crop planning?

options.A: Preparing alternative crop and farm-management options for delayed monsoon, long dry spells or other adverse seasonal conditions
options.B: Planting only one crop every year

questions.explanation: Contingency crop planning involves preparing alternative crop and farm-management options for delayed monsoon, long dry spells or other adverse seasonal conditions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the role of MGNREGA in drought resilience?

options.A: It can provide rural wage employment and support durable natural-resource assets such as water conservation, land development and soil-moisture works, subject to programme rules

questions.explanation: MGNREGA can provide rural wage employment and support durable natural-resource assets such as water conservation, land development and soil-moisture works, subject to programme rules.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the role of the National Disaster Management Authority in drought management?

options.A: It provides national-level disaster-management guidance and coordination; drought response also involves the agriculture, water, rural development and state authorities

questions.explanation: The NDMA provides national-level disaster-management guidance and coordination; drought response also involves the agriculture, water, rural development and state authorities.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which authority is responsible for drought declaration in a state?

options.A: The State Government, based on prescribed assessment procedures and applicable central/state guidelines

questions.explanation: The State Government declares drought-affected areas based on prescribed assessment procedures and applicable central/state guidelines; the Union Government has roles in assessment and assistance.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the importance of drought early-warning systems?

options.A: They help governments, farmers and communities take preventive action before severe impacts occur, reducing crop losses and protecting drinking-water supplies
options.D: They replace the need for water conservation

questions.explanation: Drought early-warning systems help governments, farmers and communities take preventive action before severe impacts occur, reducing crop losses and protecting drinking-water supplies.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a flood?

options.A: The inundation of normally dry land by water, often due to river overflow, intense rainfall, storm surge, dam or embankment failure, or inadequate urban drainage
options.B: A prolonged period of low rainfall

questions.explanation: A flood is the inundation of normally dry land by water, often due to river overflow, intense rainfall, storm surge, dam or embankment failure, or inadequate urban drainage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is riverine flooding?

options.A: Flooding that occurs when a river or stream exceeds its channel capacity and spreads onto adjacent land
options.B: Flooding caused by intense rainfall before it reaches a river
options.D: Flooding caused by a dam break

questions.explanation: Riverine flooding occurs when a river or stream exceeds its channel capacity and spreads onto adjacent land.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is flash flooding?

options.A: A rapid rise of water, often within minutes or hours of intense rainfall, cloudbursts, dam releases or sudden drainage failure
options.C: A coastal flood caused by tides
options.D: A flood caused by snowmelt only

questions.explanation: Flash flooding is a rapid rise of water, often within minutes or hours of intense rainfall, cloudbursts, dam releases or sudden drainage failure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is urban flooding?

options.A: Flooding in built-up areas when rainfall exceeds the capacity of drainage systems or water cannot infiltrate or flow away because of urban development and drainage obstruction
options.B: Flooding caused by river overflow in rural areas
options.D: Flooding caused by glacial lake outbursts

questions.explanation: Urban flooding occurs in built-up areas when rainfall exceeds the capacity of drainage systems or water cannot infiltrate or flow away because of urban development and drainage obstruction.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is coastal flooding?

options.A: Inundation of coastal land due to storm surges, high tides, waves, sea-level rise or combinations of these factors
options.C: Flooding caused by urban drainage failure
options.D: Flooding caused by a dam break

questions.explanation: Coastal flooding is the inundation of coastal land due to storm surges, high tides, waves, sea-level rise or combinations of these factors.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a pluvial flood?

options.A: Flooding caused by intense rainfall accumulating over land before it reaches a river or other watercourse
options.B: Flooding caused by rivers overflowing their banks
options.D: Flooding caused by a glacial lake outburst

questions.explanation: A pluvial flood is flooding caused by intense rainfall accumulating over land before it reaches a river or other watercourse.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a fluvial flood?

options.A: Flooding caused by rivers or streams overflowing their banks
options.B: Flooding caused by intense rainfall accumulating over land
options.D: Flooding caused by urban drainage failure

questions.explanation: A fluvial flood is flooding caused by rivers or streams overflowing their banks.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a glacial lake outburst flood (GLOF)?

options.A: A sudden release of water from a glacial lake, often after failure of an ice or moraine dam
options.B: A flood caused by a river overflowing its banks
options.C: A flood caused by intense urban rainfall
options.D: A flood caused by a storm surge

questions.explanation: A GLOF is a sudden release of water from a glacial lake, often after failure of an ice or moraine dam.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a major cause of floods listed in the notes?

options.A: Extreme or prolonged rainfall

questions.explanation: Major causes include extreme or prolonged rainfall, cyclones, snow or glacier melt, saturated soil, high tides and storm surges, dam or embankment failure, deforestation, siltation, encroachment on floodplains and inadequate urban drainage.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a floodplain?

options.A: A relatively flat area next to a river that is naturally subject to periodic inundation
options.C: A coastal area with no flooding

questions.explanation: A floodplain is a relatively flat area next to a river that is naturally subject to periodic inundation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a flood hydrograph?

options.A: A graph showing how river discharge changes over time in response to rainfall or another event
options.C: A graph of temperature versus rainfall

questions.explanation: A flood hydrograph is a graph showing how river discharge changes over time in response to rainfall or another event.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What does a 100-year flood return period mean?

options.A: It has about a 1% chance of being equalled or exceeded in any given year, not a guarantee that it occurs only once in 100 years
options.B: It occurs exactly once every 100 years
options.C: It has a 100% chance of occurring each year

questions.explanation: A 100-year flood has about a 1% chance of being equalled or exceeded in any given year, not a guarantee that it occurs only once in 100 years.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a dam-break flood?

options.A: A flood caused by the sudden or uncontrolled release of water following failure or serious malfunction of a dam
options.B: A flood caused by a river overflowing its banks
options.C: A flood caused by urban drainage failure
options.D: A flood caused by a storm surge

questions.explanation: A dam-break flood is a flood caused by the sudden or uncontrolled release of water following failure or serious malfunction of a dam.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why can deforestation increase flood risk?

options.A: Loss of vegetation can reduce interception and infiltration, increase runoff and erosion, and raise sediment loads, although flood outcomes also depend on rainfall, soils, terrain and river-basin conditions
options.C: Deforestation has no effect on runoff

questions.explanation: Loss of vegetation can reduce interception and infiltration, increase runoff and erosion, and raise sediment loads, although flood outcomes also depend on rainfall, soils, terrain and river-basin conditions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why do wetlands reduce flood risk?

options.A: Wetlands can store and slow excess water, reduce peak flows and provide natural buffers, depending on their condition and connectivity
options.C: Wetlands have no effect on floods

questions.explanation: Wetlands can store and slow excess water, reduce peak flows and provide natural buffers, depending on their condition and connectivity.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following is a major impact of floods?

options.A: Deaths and injuries, displacement, damage to homes and infrastructure, crop and livestock losses, water contamination, disease risks, erosion, livelihood disruption and economic losses

questions.explanation: Major impacts include deaths and injuries, displacement, damage to homes and infrastructure, crop and livestock losses, water contamination, disease risks, erosion, livelihood disruption and economic losses.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is flood forecasting?

options.A: The use of rainfall, river-flow, reservoir, terrain and hydrological data to estimate the likelihood, timing, location and severity of flooding
options.C: The evacuation of people during a flood

questions.explanation: Flood forecasting is the use of rainfall, river-flow, reservoir, terrain and hydrological data to estimate the likelihood, timing, location and severity of flooding.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which national agency provides river-flood forecasts in India?

options.A: The Central Water Commission (CWC)

questions.explanation: The Central Water Commission (CWC) is the principal central agency for river-flood forecasting and hydrological observation in India.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the role of the National Disaster Response Force (NDRF)?

options.A: It provides specialised response to natural and human-made disasters, including search, rescue and relief operations during floods

questions.explanation: The NDRF provides specialised response to natural and human-made disasters, including search, rescue and relief operations during floods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is floodplain zoning?

options.A: Regulating land use in flood-prone areas according to flood risk to reduce exposure of people, buildings and critical infrastructure

questions.explanation: Floodplain zoning is regulating land use in flood-prone areas according to flood risk to reduce exposure of people, buildings and critical infrastructure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is an embankment?

options.A: An engineered raised structure built along a river or coast to contain or redirect water; it requires maintenance and does not eliminate flood risk

questions.explanation: An embankment is an engineered raised structure built along a river or coast to contain or redirect water; it requires maintenance and does not eliminate flood risk.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the difference between structural and non-structural flood management?

options.A: Structural measures include dams, embankments, drainage and retention basins; non-structural measures include zoning, forecasting, warning, insurance, evacuation planning and public awareness
options.B: Structural measures include zoning; non-structural measures include dams
options.D: Structural measures are only for coastal floods

questions.explanation: Structural measures include dams, embankments, drainage and retention basins; non-structural measures include zoning, forecasting, warning, insurance, evacuation planning and public awareness.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: How can cities reduce urban flooding?

options.A: Protect lakes, wetlands and storm-water drains; restore natural drainage; prevent encroachment; increase permeable surfaces; create retention areas; maintain drains; and use risk-informed land-use planning

questions.explanation: Cities can reduce urban flooding by protecting lakes, wetlands and storm-water drains; restoring natural drainage; preventing encroachment; increasing permeable surfaces; creating retention areas; maintaining drains; and using risk-informed land-use planning.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Why should flood warnings be linked to evacuation plans?

options.A: A warning reduces risk only when people understand it and can act through timely evacuation, safe shelters, accessible routes and support for vulnerable groups

questions.explanation: A warning reduces risk only when people understand it and can act through timely evacuation, safe shelters, accessible routes and support for vulnerable groups.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is the importance of flood-resilient infrastructure?

options.A: It is designed, located and maintained to withstand or recover from flood hazards while keeping essential services functioning
options.C: It is designed only for earthquakes
options.D: It eliminates the need for flood warnings

questions.explanation: Flood-resilient infrastructure is designed, located and maintained to withstand or recover from flood hazards while keeping essential services functioning.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate adaptation?

options.A: The process of adjustment in human or natural systems in response to actual or expected climate and its effects, to moderate harm or exploit beneficial opportunities

questions.explanation: Climate adaptation is the process of adjustment in human or natural systems in response to actual or expected climate and its effects, to moderate harm or exploit beneficial opportunities.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate resilience?

options.A: The capacity of social, economic and ecological systems to cope with a hazardous event or trend, respond or reorganise, and maintain essential functions
options.B: The ability to prevent all climate impacts
options.C: The total greenhouse-gas emissions of a country
options.D: The average temperature of a region

questions.explanation: Climate resilience is the capacity of social, economic and ecological systems to cope with a hazardous event or trend, respond or reorganise, and maintain essential functions.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is adaptive capacity?

options.A: The ability of people, institutions and systems to adjust to potential damage, take advantage of opportunities or respond to consequences
options.B: The total greenhouse-gas emissions of a country
options.C: The physical presence of people in hazard-prone areas
options.D: The degree to which a system is affected by climate

questions.explanation: Adaptive capacity is the ability of people, institutions and systems to adjust to potential damage, take advantage of opportunities or respond to consequences.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is vulnerability to climate change?

options.A: The propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected, shaped by exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity
options.B: The total greenhouse-gas emissions of a country
options.C: The average temperature of a region
options.D: The ability to prevent all climate impacts

questions.explanation: Vulnerability to climate change is the propensity or predisposition to be adversely affected, shaped by exposure, sensitivity and adaptive capacity.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is exposure in the context of climate vulnerability?

options.A: The presence of people, livelihoods, species, ecosystems, infrastructure or assets in places that could be adversely affected
options.B: The degree to which a system is affected by climate
options.C: The ability to adjust to climate impacts
options.D: The total greenhouse-gas emissions of a country

questions.explanation: Exposure is the presence of people, livelihoods, species, ecosystems, infrastructure or assets in places that could be adversely affected.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is sensitivity in the context of climate vulnerability?

options.A: The degree to which a system is affected, either adversely or beneficially, by climate variability or change
options.B: The presence of people in hazard-prone areas
options.C: The ability to adjust to climate impacts
options.D: The total greenhouse-gas emissions of a country

questions.explanation: Sensitivity is the degree to which a system is affected, either adversely or beneficially, by climate variability or change.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is maladaptation?

options.A: An action intended to reduce climate risk that unintentionally increases vulnerability, emissions or risk for other people, places or future periods

questions.explanation: Maladaptation is an action intended to reduce climate risk that unintentionally increases vulnerability, emissions or risk for other people, places or future periods.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is ecosystem-based adaptation?

options.A: Using biodiversity and ecosystem services, such as forests, wetlands, mangroves and watersheds, to help people adapt to climate impacts

questions.explanation: Ecosystem-based adaptation uses biodiversity and ecosystem services, such as forests, wetlands, mangroves and watersheds, to help people adapt to climate impacts.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is community-based adaptation?

options.A: An approach that places local communities, their knowledge, priorities and participation at the centre of climate-risk assessment and adaptation planning
options.B: An approach led only by national governments
options.C: An approach that excludes local knowledge
options.D: An approach focused only on engineering

questions.explanation: Community-based adaptation places local communities, their knowledge, priorities and participation at the centre of climate-risk assessment and adaptation planning.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a nature-based solution?

options.A: An action that protects, sustainably manages or restores natural or modified ecosystems to address societal challenges while benefiting people and biodiversity

questions.explanation: A nature-based solution is an action that protects, sustainably manages or restores natural or modified ecosystems to address societal challenges while benefiting people and biodiversity.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is climate-proofing?

options.A: Integrating climate-risk considerations into the design, construction, operation and maintenance of policies, projects and infrastructure
options.D: Building only during the dry season

questions.explanation: Climate-proofing is integrating climate-risk considerations into the design, construction, operation and maintenance of policies, projects and infrastructure.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a climate risk assessment?

options.A: A systematic assessment of climate hazards, exposure, vulnerability and potential consequences to inform decisions and prioritise action
options.B: A weather forecast for the next day
options.D: A list of adaptation measures only

questions.explanation: A climate risk assessment is a systematic assessment of climate hazards, exposure, vulnerability and potential consequences to inform decisions and prioritise action.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following are important adaptation measures in agriculture?

options.A: Drought- and heat-tolerant varieties, crop diversification, altered sowing calendars, agroforestry, soil-moisture conservation, weather advisories, crop insurance and efficient irrigation

questions.explanation: Important adaptation measures in agriculture include drought- and heat-tolerant varieties, crop diversification, altered sowing calendars, agroforestry, soil-moisture conservation, weather advisories, crop insurance and efficient irrigation.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following are important adaptation measures in water management?

options.A: Rainwater harvesting, watershed restoration, groundwater recharge, protection of tanks and wetlands, water budgeting, efficient irrigation and wastewater reuse

questions.explanation: Important adaptation measures in water management include rainwater harvesting, watershed restoration, groundwater recharge, protection of tanks and wetlands, water budgeting, efficient irrigation and wastewater reuse.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following are important adaptation measures in cities?

options.A: Urban green spaces, cool roofs, heat action plans, flood-resilient drainage, wetland protection, permeable surfaces, early-warning systems and climate-sensitive urban planning

questions.explanation: Important adaptation measures in cities include urban green spaces, cool roofs, heat action plans, flood-resilient drainage, wetland protection, permeable surfaces, early-warning systems and climate-sensitive urban planning.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following are important adaptation measures for coastal areas?

options.A: Mangrove and dune restoration, coastal setback and risk-informed zoning, resilient infrastructure, cyclone shelters, early warnings and livelihood diversification

questions.explanation: Important adaptation measures for coastal areas include mangrove and dune restoration, coastal setback and risk-informed zoning, resilient infrastructure, cyclone shelters, early warnings and livelihood diversification.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: Which of the following are important adaptation measures for public health?

options.A: Heat-health action plans, early warnings, cooling centres, safe drinking water, disease surveillance, resilient health facilities and targeted support for outdoor workers and vulnerable populations
options.D: Reducing access to safe drinking water

questions.explanation: Important adaptation measures for public health include heat-health action plans, early warnings, cooling centres, safe drinking water, disease surveillance, resilient health facilities and targeted support for outdoor workers and vulnerable populations.

questions.subject: General Knowledge
questions.question: What is a Heat Action Plan?

options.A: A preparedness and response framework that uses heat-risk information, public communication, health-system readiness and targeted measures to reduce heat-related illness and deaths
